archetype.name: Rebuilding (first-year reset)
archetype.definition: A 1-7 team in Jeff Hafley's first season whose defense has fallen to the bottom of the league in efficiency and whose run-first offense can't score enough to cover for it, so the rest of the year is about finding pieces, not chasing a playoff spot.

report.headline: Mostly earned: a last-ranked defense and a stalled passing game, not bad luck.
report.take:
Miami is a run-first team trying to protect a quarterback and a defense it can't fully trust. Malik Willis has started every game, and the offense leans away from him: a pass rate over expected of -9.7 is 31st in the league. That is less a philosophy than a workaround. Willis holds the ball (3.056 seconds to throw), the line gives up pressure on 23.3% of dropbacks, and the sack rate of 9.3% is 30th. The result is 15.8 points a game, 31st, with the passing game living on a few good afternoons like the 28-25 win over the Jets rather than any repeatable weekly floor.

The defense is the bigger story, and it is worse than its yardage suggests. Miami allows 329 yards a game, 13th, which looks respectable until you see the efficiency: 0.110 EPA per play allowed and a 48.4% success rate allowed are both dead last, and opponents convert 47.4% of third downs (29th). Offenses don't need explosive volume against this group. They stay on schedule, work tight ends and backs underneath (TEs draw 29% of targets against Miami against a league share of 24.1%), and finish drives. With 12 sacks (31st) and 7 takeaways (29th), the defense isn't ending possessions on its own either. This continues a slide that was already visible in 2025, when the unit ranked 25th in EPA allowed.

Is the record a fluke? Only at the margins. Wins over expected sits at -1.03 and the point differential implies 2 wins, so one extra win's worth of close-game bad luck is buried in the 1-7. Special teams at -2.7 EPA a game (28th) has also cost field position. But netEpa of -0.177 is 30th, the offense is 26th and the defense 32nd. This is a bottom-three team playing like one, with a modest amount of luck on top.

The path forward is narrow. The schedule ahead runs through Buffalo twice plus Denver, Chicago and Green Bay, all winning teams, so the realistic wins are Indianapolis this week, the Jets at home and a winless Chargers team. A first-year staff will be judged less on the record than on whether the defense stops bleeding success rate and whether the run blocking, which shows real promise, can carry an offense that won't throw.

strengths.title: Run blocking that creates early yards
strengths.body: Miami's backs average 2.99 yards before contact, third best in the league, and the line converts 73.3% of short-yardage tries (10th). When the blocking holds, the run game can carry a game, as in the 217-yard day against Cincinnati. The catch is that it is boom-or-bust: a 26.3% stuff rate (30th) means too many runs die at the line. The push is real and should last, but the overall run EPA won't climb until the busted plays shrink.

strengths.title: Outside receivers kept in check
strengths.body: Opponents' top two wideouts have scored well under their usual output against Miami: WR1s at 5.2 PPR points below average and WR2s at 2.7 below, both third best. Offenses have also aimed away from receivers, with WRs drawing 49% of targets against a league share of 58%. Treat it cautiously. The WR1 EPA per target is 0.47 (28th), so the volume suppression is partly about where offenses chose to throw, and eight games of opponent mix can swing a rank like this.

concerns.title: A defense that loses every down
concerns.body: The 48.4% success rate allowed and 0.110 EPA per play allowed are both last in the league, and the 47.4% third-down rate allowed means drives rarely end early. The damage comes underneath and over the middle: tight ends post 0.76 EPA per target against Miami and slot-type WR3s 0.97, both 32nd. This is a structural flaw, not a schedule quirk, and it extends a decline from 2025.

concerns.title: Long holds behind a leaky line
concerns.body: Willis takes 3.056 seconds to throw and the line allows pressure on 23.3% of dropbacks (28th), a pairing that produces a 9.3% sack rate, 30th. That has sacks of five in two separate games and a 24-sack total through eight. Part of it is the quarterback's style and part is the line, which also draws 4.1 penalties a game (27th). It is why the staff passes so little, and it caps the offense's ceiling.

concerns.title: No pass rush, no takeaways
concerns.body: Twelve sacks (31st) and seven takeaways (29th) mean the defense almost never flips a possession on its own. Pressure arrives on 19.4% of dropbacks (22nd), so quarterbacks have time to work the soft middle. Takeaways can swing on luck, but a weak rush keeps the floor low.

trend.note: After lopsided early losses to the 49ers and Chiefs, the margins tightened into one-score games and the Jets win, but the 19-9 loss to Detroit, with 87 penalty yards and Willis completing 13 of 25, showed the same ceiling. The team plays closer now without playing better.

nextGame.headline: Two bottom-tier offenses, and Miami's run game meets Indy's weak spot
nextGame.body:
This is a near coin flip between two of the league's least efficient teams: the Book has Indianapolis by 2.5 with a 40.5 total. The matchup that favors Miami is its own identity. The Colts rank last in rush EPA allowed, and lead backs post their best numbers against them (RB1 EPA per play 32nd, PPR over average 32nd), which suits a team that runs as often as Miami and hands Ollie Gordon II most of the carries. The danger runs the other way, too: Indy's run game is sixth in rush EPA against a Miami rush defense that is 23rd. Something also has to give when the Colts' 31st-ranked passing offense meets Miami's 31st-ranked pass defense. Daniel Jones has started every game for Indianapolis, and the Colts have turned it over far more than they've taken it away, at -1.2 a game.

Availability tilts toward Miami if Willis plays. He is questionable with a groin injury after a full workload, and the dossier shows no other quarterback throwing a pass this year, so his status is the biggest swing in the game. TE Will Kacmarek is questionable, RB Jaylen Wright and CB Darrell Baker Jr. are out. Indianapolis is thinner where Miami wants to attack: starting LB Akeem Davis-Gaither, S A.J. Haulcy and CB Justin Walley are out, OT Jalen Travis is expected to miss two to four weeks, WR Alec Pierce is on injured reserve, and TE Mo Alie-Cox is questionable.

waysToWin.title: Run straight at Indy's front
waysToWin.body: The Colts allow the worst rush EPA in the league and are missing a starting linebacker and safety. Miami's line creates 2.99 yards before contact, so steady Gordon carries can keep Willis out of long-yardage dropbacks, where the sacks pile up. A game like the Cincinnati one, where the run game carried the offense, is the template.

waysToWin.title: Tight end targets in the middle
waysToWin.body: Indianapolis ranks 27th in EPA allowed to tight ends and 28th in TE PPR over average, and losing a linebacker and a safety opens the same middle of the field. Greg Dulcich is second on the team in targets, giving Willis a short, quick read that avoids his tendency to hold the ball.

waysToWin.title: Let the Colts' passing game stall
waysToWin.body: Indy's pass offense is 31st in EPA and it gives the ball away at -1.2 a game in turnover differential. Even a defense with Miami's weak rush can win this game if it forces Jones to throw on third down rather than run.

waysToLose.title: Colts run game controls the clock
waysToLose.body: Indianapolis is sixth in rush EPA and seventh in run success, and Miami's defense allows the league's worst success rate overall. If the Colts stay on schedule on early downs, they avoid the passing game that would hand Miami the edge. Indy already averages more time of possession than Miami, which would mean fewer Miami possessions in a low total.

waysToLose.title: Field position lost on special teams
waysToLose.body: The Colts are +1.61 EPA a game on special teams (6th) while Miami is -2.7 (28th). In a game the Book expects to be close and low scoring, a few hidden yards on returns or a missed kick could decide it.

waysToLose.title: Willis limited or out
waysToLose.body: Willis is questionable with a groin injury, and his legs are part of the offense. A hobbled Willis holding the ball behind a line with a 9.3% sack rate is the quickest way for Miami's drives to die. Indy's 27th-ranked pressure rate softens that, but its fifth-ranked third-down defense can still stall the offense.

nextGame.watch: Ollie Gordon II's early-down carries against a Colts front missing Davis-Gaither: if Miami is running for steady gains in the first half, it controls the game.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect more of the same with a bit less bad luck. The -1.03 wins over expected points to a close game or two breaking Miami's way later, but the differential only implies 2 wins, so there is no hidden good team here. The run blocking's ability to create yards before contact should hold, and the defense's efficiency allowed is so extreme that it likely drifts off the bottom. Outside receivers being held well under their averages probably won't last. Neither will the passing game's occasional big days, given the sack rate and how little the offense throws.

The schedule is the ceiling. Buffalo twice, Denver, Chicago and Green Bay are all winning teams, and New England is above .500. Indianapolis, the Jets at home and the winless Chargers are the realistic chances, so the season most likely ends with two to four wins. How often the defense gets off the field on third down will decide whether Hafley's first year looks like a foundation or a teardown.
swingFactors: Willis's groin and the lack of a proven backup
Whether the defense's third-down and success-rate collapse eases
Winning the soft spots: IND, NYJ at home, LAC

confidence.note: Eight games of a consistent profile, but QB health and a first-year staff add uncertainty.
